mcqs.question: Why does combination generation use a `start` index that only ever moves forward, instead of trying every unused element like permutation generation does?
options: It makes the recursion terminate faster in every case
It reduces the memory used by the path list
Since order doesn't matter for a combination, allowing backward reconsideration would generate the same set of values more than once, in different orders
It's required so that duplicate values in the input are automatically handled
mcqs.explanation: Because {1,2} and {2,1} are the same combination, ever looking backward to reconsider an earlier element would regenerate a set of values that's already been produced in a different order — the forward-only start index is precisely what prevents that. It's about avoiding same-value reordering, not primarily a speed or memory optimization, and it's separate from duplicate-value handling.

mcqs.question: In "choose k of n", a branch has 2 elements in its path and needs 3 more, but only 2 candidates remain from the current index to n. What should happen?
options: The branch is pruned immediately, since 2 remaining candidates can't produce the 3 more elements needed
The branch continues normally and simply returns fewer combinations than expected
The branch should restart from index 1 to find more candidates
The branch is only prunable if k equals n exactly
mcqs.explanation: Once the count of remaining candidates falls below what's still needed to reach size k, no completion is possible from that point on, so the branch can be cut immediately rather than explored to a wasted leaf. This prune is unconditional and doesn't require k to equal n — it applies whenever the arithmetic makes success impossible.

mcqs.question: In Combination Sum, why does the recursive call after including `candidates[i]` pass `i` rather than `i + 1`?
options: Because passing `i` is required to keep the results sorted
Because unlimited reuse means the same element can be chosen again on the very next recursive call
It's a typo-prone convention with no functional difference from `i + 1`
Because it prevents the target sum from ever going negative
mcqs.explanation: Passing `i` keeps that same candidate eligible for the very next pick, which is exactly what unlimited reuse of an element requires — candidates before `i` are still permanently excluded, only the just-chosen one can repeat. Using `i + 1` instead is precisely the change that forbids reuse, as seen in "choose k of n" and Combination Sum II.

mcqs.question: Combination Sum II forbids reusing an element but the candidate list itself has duplicate values. What two separate mechanisms are needed?
options: A hash set to track used values, and nothing else
Sorting alone; sorting automatically prevents both reuse and duplicate combinations
Recursing with `i + 1` to forbid reuse of a physical element, plus a sort-and-skip check to forbid duplicate combinations from equal-valued elements at the same level
Recursing with `i` to allow flexibility, plus a post-processing de-duplication pass on the final result
mcqs.explanation: The two constraints are independent: `i + 1` (not `i`) stops the same physical element from being picked twice, while the sort-then-skip-equal-at-this-level guard stops two equal-valued elements from each starting an identical branch. Neither one alone solves both problems, and post-processing de-duplication is unnecessary if the recursion itself is written correctly.

mcqs.question: A combination-sum implementation recurses with `backtrack(start, ...)` instead of `backtrack(i, ...)` or `backtrack(i+1, ...)` after choosing `candidates[i]`. What's the observable symptom?
options: The recursion crashes with a stack overflow
The output contains the same set of values appearing more than once, in different orders
The target sum is never reached because remaining shrinks too fast
No symptom — `start` and `i` are interchangeable in this position
mcqs.explanation: Reusing the incoming `start` instead of the current `i` lets the next level reconsider candidates before the one just chosen, which reproduces the same values as a separate, differently-ordered branch — a duplicate-by-reordering bug, not a crash or an incorrect sum. The recursive call must always derive its next start point from `i`, the index just processed, not from the value it received.

mcqs.question: Subsets, "choose k of n", and Combination Sum all share the same forward-only start-index scaffold. What actually differs between them?
options: The stopping rule (what ends a branch as a successful answer) and, where applicable, the pruning condition used to end a branch early as dead
Whether recursion or iteration is used to implement the search
Whether the input needs to be sorted first — only one of the three benefits from sorting
Whether duplicate values in the input are possible — only one of the three can contain duplicates
mcqs.explanation: All three use the identical include/skip-forward recursive skeleton; what changes is purely what counts as a finished, valid answer (end of input, a target size, or a target sum) and what lets a branch be cut early as provably dead. All three are implemented recursively, all three can benefit from sorting, and duplicate values are a concern for any of them depending on the input.
